6 Light

6.1 Reflection

Key words: angle of incidence · angle of reflection · incident ray · law of reflection · normal · perpendicular · plane mirror · protractor · ray diagram · rays · reflection · set square

Reflection from a plane mirror

Most of the mirrors you use are plane mirrors. 'Plane' means flat. A reflection from a surface that is not plane — the back of a spoon, for example — is distorted.

Light travels in straight lines called rays. When you draw a light ray, always use a ruler and put an arrowhead on the ray to show its direction.

A light ray arriving at a mirror is called the incident ray. The incident ray makes an angle with the mirror, but you do not measure that angle from the mirror itself. You measure it from a line that is perpendicular to the mirror. That line is called the normal. In physics and maths, 'normal' means perpendicular, or at right angles, to something.

Drawing a ray diagram

  1. Draw the incident ray and the mirror. Sometimes this is done for you.
  2. Use a ruler to make the incident ray meet the mirror.
  3. Use a protractor or set square to draw the normal, perpendicular to the mirror at the point where the incident ray meets the surface. The normal is usually drawn as a dashed line so it is not confused with a light ray.
  4. Use a protractor to measure the angle between the incident ray and the normal. This is the angle of incidence, i.
  5. Measure an equal angle on the other side of the normal. This is the angle of reflection, r. Draw the reflected ray coming away from the mirror at this angle, with an arrowhead on it.

These diagrams are called ray diagrams because they show what happens to the light rays during reflection.

Remember: the law of reflection — the angle of reflection is equal to the angle of incidence. In physics, a law is something that always applies.

Using reflection

Mirrors can be used to see behind us.

Light from the Sun is reflected from the cyclist. That is the incident ray on the mirror. The reflected ray from the mirror goes to the driver's eye.

Measuring angles of incidence and reflection

You will need: a ray box with power supply · a plane mirror and a support to hold it vertical · plain paper · pencil · ruler · protractor. Make the room as dark as possible.

Method

  1. Place the plane mirror vertically at one side of the white paper and mark the position of the front of the mirror with a pencil.
  2. Use the protractor to draw a normal line at the surface of the mirror.
  3. Use the ray box to direct a ray of light onto the mirror, where the normal meets the mirror surface.
  4. Mark the positions of the incident and reflected rays on the paper with a pencil.
  5. Turn the ray box off, remove the mirror, and use the pencil marks to construct the ray diagram. Draw the normal with the protractor.
  6. Measure and record the angle of incidence, i, and the angle of reflection, r.
  7. Repeat for at least four more different angles.

In this experiment the independent variable is the angle of incidence and the dependent variable is the angle of reflection. A graph of r against i gives a straight line through the origin.

6.2 Refraction

Key words: angle of refraction · away from the normal · bent · distorted · lenses · medium · refraction · towards the normal

What refraction is

When you look through a glass of water or a wet window, you cannot see clearly. The background looks distorted — changed to be less clear. This happens because of refraction.

The material that light passes through is called a medium. Air, glass and water are all media for light.

MediumSpeed of light in km/s
air300 000
water225 000
glass200 000

Light travels more slowly in water or glass than in air, and this change of speed can make the light change direction.

Imagine you are moving at a constant speed on roller skates and the skate on one foot runs onto grass. You change direction, because one skate is now moving more slowly than the other. The same thing happens to a ray of light: one side of the ray slows down first, so the ray changes direction.

Remember: refraction of light is defined as the change in direction of light on passing from one medium into another because of a change in speed.

Air into glass or water

The light slows down, so it is bent towards the normal. The refracted ray is closer to the normal than the incident ray would have been if it had carried straight on. The angle of incidence is greater than the angle of refraction. Both angles are measured from the normal.

Glass or water into air

The light speeds up, so it is bent away from the normal. Here the angle of refraction is greater than the angle of incidence.

Refraction in everyday life

Each drop of water on a window refracts light in a different direction, which makes it very hard to see through. Windscreen wipers remove the drops so that all the refraction from the glass is in the same direction.

Refraction is also useful. A lens is a curved piece of glass designed to refract light in a known way. Lenses are used in our eyes, in cameras and in the glasses that people wear.

Refraction effects

Effect 1 — the appearing coin. Put a coin at the bottom of an opaque cup and position yourself so the coin is just out of view behind the edge. Pour water in carefully. The coin comes into view, because light from the coin is refracted as it leaves the water.

Effect 2 — the broken pencil. Rest a pencil at an angle in a glass about three-quarters full of water and look from the side. The pencil appears broken at the water surface.

Effect 3 — water and oil. Half fill the glass with water, then gently pour cooking oil on top. The pencil now appears to bend twice, which tells you the speed of light in oil is different again.

Drawing accurate ray diagrams

You will need: a ray box and power supply · a glass block · plain paper · pencil · ruler · protractor. Make the room as dark as possible.

Draw around the glass block, shine the ray in at an angle, mark the incident ray in two places and the emerging ray in two places, then lift the block off and join the marks. Draw a normal at both surfaces and measure the angles. Include an angle of incidence of zero: the ray then passes straight through without bending.

6.3 Making rainbows

Key words: dispersion · prism · spectrum · triangular

Newton's discovery about light

In 1666, Isaac Newton showed that white light could be split into different colours. He let sunlight through a hole, passed it through a glass block shaped like a triangle, and shone the colours onto a screen.

The spectrum

The range of colours seen in white light is called a spectrum. In the spectrum the colours are not separate; they merge from one to another.

Most people now agree there are seven colours. In order:

red · orange · yellow · green · blue · indigo · violet

You can remember the order with the made-up name 'ROY G. BIV'.

Dispersion

Dispersion means splitting light into different colours. It happens because each colour in white light is refracted through a slightly different angle. A triangular prism shows this well.

Remember: violet light is refracted through the largest angle and red light through the smallest angle.

Rainbows

A rainbow is formed when drops of water in the air cause dispersion of light, and the light is also reflected inside the drops. For you to see a rainbow:

  • the Sun must be shining, to provide bright light
  • there must be rain or small drops of water in the air, to cause dispersion
  • the Sun must be behind you, because the water drops reflect the light inside them.

Making a rainbow

You will need: a ray box and suitable power supply · a triangular glass prism · a piece of white paper or card to use as a screen.

Safety: do not put your eye closer to the prism than about half a metre. The light becomes very bright and could damage your eye.

Adjust the ray box and the screen until you see the colours on the screen, then move the screen closer and further away and describe what changes.

6.4 Colours of light

Key words: absorbed · coloured filters · cyan · magenta · non-luminous · primary colours · subtraction · transmit

Primary colours

There are three colours of light from which all other colours of light can be made. These are the primary colours, and they cannot be made by mixing any other colours of light:

  • red · green · blue

The primary colours of light are different from the primary colours in paints, because light mixes differently from paint.

  • red + green = yellow
  • red + blue = magenta
  • blue + green = cyan
  • red + green + blue = white

Every colour on a phone, computer or television screen is made from combinations of these three. Most screens can display 256 different colours, made by changing the brightness of each primary colour. For example, orange is red added to green with the red brighter than the green.

Subtracting colours of light

A coloured filter is a transparent piece of coloured glass or plastic. Put in front of a white light, it transmits (lets through) only light of its own colour and absorbs all the others.

Traffic lights use three identical white lamps with a red, a yellow and a green filter in front of them. White light contains seven colours; at the red filter only red is transmitted and the other six are absorbed. This is an example of subtraction of light.

Stage lights work the same way: a white lamp inside a black case, with a coloured filter in front. Photographers sometimes use coloured filters on a camera to get different effects.

You can subtract colours until nothing is left. White light through a green filter gives green light. If that green light then meets a red filter, no light gets through at all — green is one of the colours a red filter absorbs.

Seeing colours

When you look at a non-luminous object — one that does not emit its own light — you see the light reflected from it.

The flower looks yellow because it reflects only yellow light and absorbs the other six colours of white light.

  • A white object reflects all the colours in white light equally.
  • A black object absorbs all the colours and reflects none.

A red cube appears black in green light, because red objects reflect only red and absorb everything else. A blue cube appears black in red light for the same reason.

6.5 Galaxies

Key words: elliptical · galaxy · irregular · spiral · stellar dust · universe

The Milky Way

On a clear night, far from any lights, you can see a milky band across the sky. That band is part of the galaxy we live in, called the Milky Way. The word 'galaxy' comes from a Greek word for 'milky'.

The Milky Way is a spiral galaxy. Because we live inside it, we can only see one 'arm' of the spiral — the band across the sky. Most of the stars we see at night are in our own galaxy; there are an estimated 250 000 000 stars in the Milky Way, including our Sun.

Shapes of galaxies

The universe is all of space and everything in it. Other galaxies are classified by shape:

  • spiral
  • elliptical
  • irregular

The closest known galaxy to the Milky Way is the Canis Major Dwarf Galaxy, which is elliptical.

What galaxies are made of

Galaxies are made from stellar dust, gas, stars and solar systems, held together by gravity. Stellar dust is the dust found in space; the Earth is travelling through a cloud of it containing on average about one dust particle in every million cubic metres.

The gravity holding a galaxy together is very strong because galaxies have such large mass. The Milky Way is estimated to have 1 500 000 000 000 times the mass of the Sun, and even travelling at the speed of light it would take more than 100 000 years to cross from one side to the other.

Scientists counted the galaxies in one part of space and multiplied up to estimate about 100 000 000 000 galaxies in the universe. Estimates like this may not be accurate, because that part of space may not be typical and the total volume of the universe is not known accurately.

6.6 Rocks in space

Key words: asteroid belt · asteroids · craters · impacts

Asteroids

Asteroids are objects made from rock that orbit the Sun. They range in size up to 975 km across; the smallest one studied is 2 m across. Most are not regular shapes — scientists often describe them as being shaped like potatoes.

Most asteroids orbit the Sun between the orbits of Mars and Jupiter. This part of the Solar System is called the asteroid belt. There are millions of asteroids, and some of those that have been studied have been given names.

Ceres is the largest asteroid. It was discovered in 1801, and at first scientists thought it was a new planet; because it looked much smaller than a planet, the term 'asteroid' was introduced. The photograph was taken by a spacecraft in 2015. Ceres is round, 975 km in diameter, covered with craters, and has a core, a mantle and a crust like some planets. Scientists think Ceres would have become a planet if it had kept growing while the Solar System formed.

Itokawa is about 530 m long and 250 m wide. In 2005 a spacecraft collected samples from its surface — at that time the smallest asteroid to be visited. Itokawa appears to be made from lumps of rock broken off other small planets or moons by impacts. The gravity holding those lumps together is weak because the asteroid is so small, so tidal forces can change its shape when it passes a planet.

Some asteroids are made from a single piece of rock. Scientists know this because those asteroids are small and spin quickly, and their gravity would be too weak to hold separate pieces together.

Asteroids and Earth

Scientists think a large asteroid impacts the Earth on average every 130 000 years. Smaller asteroids hit much more often — the ones on this map broke apart in the atmosphere and never reached the surface.

There are two reasons why asteroids impact with Earth:

  • the Earth exerts a strong force of gravity on passing objects such as asteroids
  • many asteroids have orbits that pass relatively close to Earth.

Summary checklist

  • I can understand and describe how light is reflected from a plane mirror.
  • I can recall the law of reflection.
  • I can draw ray diagrams to show reflection of light from a plane mirror.
  • I can describe how light changes speed between air and either water or glass.
  • I can recall that a change in speed can make a light ray change direction.
  • I can recall which way light changes direction when it passes from air into glass or water, and from glass or water into air.
  • I can recall that white light is made from different colours of light.
  • I can describe how to use a prism to produce dispersion of white light.
  • I can list the seven colours of the spectrum in order starting from red.
  • I can recall the three primary colours of light and what they make when added.
  • I can explain how a coloured filter subtracts colours from white light.
  • I can explain why a non-luminous object appears to be a particular colour.
  • I can understand what galaxies are and recall the three shapes of galaxy.
  • I can recall that galaxies contain stellar dust and gas, stars and solar systems, held together by gravity.
  • I can describe what is meant by the term asteroid and recall where most asteroids are found.
  • I can know that some asteroids pass close by Earth and can, from time to time, impact Earth.
